description: Founder & AI full-stack developer building ForgePath an AI-powered exploration experience combining NASA data, interactive Martian mapping, mission history, and cosmic discovery. Skilled in GenAI, AI agents, ML, SaaS, cloud, and rapid prototyping. Looking for ambitious builders passionate about space, AI, and building something extraordinary.
summary:
Forgepath is an interactive, WebGL-powered 3D hardware atlas and mission control simulator built with Three.js and Vite. It transports school-age learners to procedural 3D environments across Mars, the Moon, and Deep Space to explore humanity's extraterrestrial machines.

Forgepath directly addresses the challenge by answering five core questions for each artifact: what was left behind, why it was built, who operated it, what engineering hazards it faced, and what science it unlocked. Rather than relying on static text, it engages students through interactive mechanical disassembly, dual-mode 3D orbital globes, official NASA imagery, and an autonomous traverse planner where learners balance scientific payoff against rover battery budgets and wheel-slip hazards.

Forgepath is important because it bridges past exploration heritage with modern missions, teaching essential systems-engineering trade-offs. By turning complex planetary telemetry into an accessible, zero-install classroom experience, it inspires the Artemis generation to become tomorrow's scientists and aerospace engineers.
details:
Forgepath is an interactive, WebGL-powered 3D hardware atlas and mission control simulator designed to introduce school-age enthusiasts to the machines humanity has left on the Moon, Mars, and in Deep Space—and the science those machines unlocked.

The project works through four integrated systems:

  1. Multi-World 3D Environments: Built with Three.js, users can transition between procedural 3D environments like Mars (Jezero Crater), featuring rust-orange basaltic topography and Rayleigh dust scattering; the Moon (Hadley-Apennine), rendering high-contrast regolith, a vacuum sky, and an Earthrise view; and Deep Space, simulating gravitational Lagrange orbits for probes like Voyager 1 and the James Webb Space Telescope.
  2. Dual-Mode 3D MiniMap and Topographic Relief: Features a 3D Orbital Globe mode with pulse-animated beacons marking historic landing sites (Apollo 11, 15, 17; Lunokhod 1; Chandrayaan-3; Perseverance; Curiosity; Pathfinder) alongside a 3D Relief Mesh mode displaying interactive wireframe elevation meshes of geological formations like Hadley Rille and the Jezero river delta.
  3. Interactive Hardware Anatomy and NASA Archive Integration: Catalogs 12 landmark artifacts across the solar system, allowing users to disassemble mechanical subsystems—such as wire-mesh wheels and laser retroreflectors—while querying the NASA Image and Video Library and Mars Rover Photos API in real-time.
  4. Mission Control Telemetry and Autonomous Route Planner: Displays real environmental data modeled after the NASA / JPL MEDA instrument suite and Apollo exosphere archives, complete with a gamified traverse planner where users balance scientific discovery against wheel slip, slope hazards, and battery margins, plus a "Student Golden Record" console for future explorers.

The project benefits learners by replacing passive reading with active inquiry, letting students take on the role of mission controllers and planetary geologists exploring 3D terrains. It teaches systems engineering trade-offs by demonstrating how real space exploration manages constraints like battery capacity and terrain hazards, celebrates extraterrestrial heritage by framing landed machines as historical monuments, and ensures classroom accessibility with lightweight procedural graphics that run smoothly at 60 FPS on low-cost school Chromebooks and tablets.

The intended impact is to target school-age students (grades 4–12), educators, and young space enthusiasts to inspire the Artemis and Mars generation by bridging historic and current missions. It democratizes NASA Open Science by translating complex planetary datasets into an intuitive visual language and cultivates a broader planetary perspective through engineering prompts and message archivers.

The technical stack utilizes JavaScript (ES6+) and HTML5/CSS3 for component architecture, Three.js and Vite for 3D procedural rendering and build tooling, and Lucide for iconography. The backend relies on Node.js and Vercel Serverless Functions alongside NASA APIs (Mars Rover Photos, Image and Video Library, and APOD), referencing scientific datasets from MEDA, ALSEP, LOLA, and MOLA, while requiring only a standard browser with WebGL support.

Creativity is driven by a Space Archaeology framework that treats spacecraft as historical storytellers through core questions about their mission, build, and engineering challenges. It merges macroscopic orbital globes with microscopic canyon wireframes, uses inquiry-driven pedagogy with open-ended reflection questions instead of dry technical specs, and applies custom Three.js shaders to replicate the realistic lighting and atmospheric dust scattering of each celestial world.

Key factors considered during development include performance and classroom bandwidth budgets to ensure fast loading times on low-bandwidth Wi-Fi, data resilience with a multi-tier fallback architecture to handle API interruptions, and a balance between scientific rigor and accessibility for younger learners. The team also ensured an international exploration scope celebrating global contribution from NASA and Soviet vehicles to India's Chandrayaan-3 and maintained deployment portability so the codebase runs identically in local development, on Vercel, or as a static GitHub Pages build.
